t.3.64.2: Surely this bird, striving in my cause, has been struck down in battle by the rākṣasa and is now giving up his life-breaths, so hard to give up.
t.3.64.1: But Rāma, seeing that vulture struck down to the ground by a cruel deed, spoke these words, full of friendship, to Saumitri.
t.3.64.4: O Jaṭāyu, if you are able to speak words once more, tell me of Sītā, may good fortune be with you, and tell me of your own slaying.
t.3.64.3: Lakṣmaṇa, the breath of life is still found in this body of his; yet, bereft of voice, he gazes up piteously.
t.3.64.5: For what reason did Rāvaṇa carry off Sītā? What wrong have I done him, that on seeing it Rāvaṇa has stolen away my beloved?
t.3.64.6: How did that lovely face of hers, bright as the moon, look then, and what words did Sītā speak at that time, O best of birds?
t.3.64.7: Of what prowess, of what form, and of what deeds is that rākṣasa? And where is his dwelling, dear father? Tell me, as I ask you earnestly.
t.3.64.8: Then, gazing up at Rāma as he lamented without pause, the stricken Jaṭāyus spoke these words to him in a voice grown very faint.
t.3.64.9: She was carried off through the sky by Rāvaṇa, lord of the Rākṣasas, who had resorted to a vast illusion thick with wind and storm-clouds.
t.3.64.10: O dear one, when I was exhausted, the night-wanderer cut off my two wings, seized Sītā, the princess of Videha, and went away facing south.
t.3.64.11: My life-breaths are failing, O Rāghava, and my sight is whirling; I see golden trees whose hair is made of uśīra grass.
t.3.64.12: In the hour in which Rāvaṇa goes away carrying off Sītā, the owner quickly regains wealth that has been lost.
t.3.64.13: That hour is called Vinda, O Kākutstha, and he did not know it; like a fish that has seized the hook, he swiftly perishes.
t.3.64.14: And you should not grieve over the daughter of Janaka; having slain that rākṣasa in battle, you will soon delight once more with Vaidehī.
t.3.64.15: As the vulture, still clear in mind, was answering Rāma, blood mingled with flesh streamed from the mouth of the dying bird.
t.3.64.16: "He is the very son of Viśravas and the brother of Vaiśravaṇa": having said this, the lord of birds released his life-breaths, so hard to hold on to.
t.3.64.17: Even as Rāma, with joined palms, was saying, "Speak, speak!", the life-breaths of the vulture left its body and went up into the sky.
t.3.64.18: Then, laying his head upon the earth and stretching out his feet, and flinging his body down, he fell upon the surface of the ground.
t.3.64.19: Seeing that red-eyed vulture lying lifeless like a mountain, Rāma, wretched with very many sorrows, spoke to Saumitri.
t.3.64.20: Dwelling happily for many years in the Daṇḍaka forest, the haunt of the Rākṣasas, this bird used to roam about here.
t.3.64.21: He who had lived many years and stood strong for so long now lies here slain today; for Time is indeed hard to overcome.
t.3.64.23: Having given up the great kingdom of the vultures, inherited from his father and forefathers, this lord of birds has laid down his life for my sake.
t.3.64.22: Look, Lakṣmaṇa: this vulture, my helper, has been struck down by the mightier Rāvaṇa, surely while he tried to shield Sītā.
t.3.64.24: O Saumitri, good beings who walk the path of dharma, heroic and ready to give refuge, are surely seen everywhere, even among those born of animal wombs.
t.3.64.25: The grief born of Sītā's abduction has not come upon me so heavily, gentle one, as the death of the vulture that fell for my sake, O scorcher of foes.
t.3.64.26: Just as the glorious and greatly renowned King Daśaratha is worthy of my worship and honour, so too is this lord of birds.
t.3.64.27: O Saumitri, bring firewood; I shall kindle a fire by friction. I wish to cremate the king of vultures, who has met his death for my sake.
t.3.64.28: I shall place upon the funeral pyre this lord of the world of birds; O Saumitri, I shall cremate him, slain by the fierce rākṣasa.
t.3.64.29: The destination reached by those devoted to sacrifice, the destination of one who keeps the sacred fires kindled, the destination of those who never turn back, and the destination of those who make gifts of land.
t.3.64.31: Having spoken thus, the righteous Rāma, grief-stricken, placed the lord of birds upon the blazing pyre and cremated him as though he were his own kinsman.
t.3.64.30: With my leave, go to the unsurpassed worlds, O king of vultures, O mighty-spirited one; and, having received your funeral rites from me, depart.
t.3.64.33: Having taken out the flesh of the rohi deer and cut it into pieces, the greatly renowned Rāma gave it to the bird on the lovely, green grassy ground.
t.3.64.32: Then the mighty Rāma, together with Saumitri, went into the forest, and having slain stout, great rohi deer, spread out offerings for that bird.
t.3.64.34: That which the twice-born recite for a mortal who has departed, that prayer for his going to heaven, Rāma swiftly murmured for him.
t.3.64.35: Then the two sons of the best of men went to the river Godāvarī, and both of them offered water to that king of vultures.
t.3.64.36: That king of vultures, who had performed a glorious and most difficult deed and was struck down in battle, was then given the funeral rites by one like a great sage, and went to his own holy and auspicious destination.
